key_terms.meaning: Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ/aⱼ, the wave leaving port i over the wave entering port j, with every other port matched; |Sᵢⱼ|² is a power ratio.
Reciprocal: S = Sᵀ. Lossless: S†S = I, so every column has unit length and the columns are orthogonal.
Branch on the broad wall (E-plane, series): outputs 180° apart. Branch on the narrow wall (H-plane, shunt): outputs in phase.
E-arm and H-arm on one junction; S = (1/√2)[0 0 1 1; 0 0 1 −1; 1 1 0 0; 1 −1 0 0]. H-arm gives the sum, E-arm the difference; both pairs isolated.
C = 10 log(P₁/P₃), D = 10 log(P₃/P₄), I = 10 log(P₁/P₄) = C + D, all in dB.
A 1.5λg ring of √2 Z₀ line with arcs λg/4, 3λg/4, λg/4, λg/4 between ports 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 4–1; port 1 is the sum port, port 3 the difference port, 1 and 3 are isolated.
Two λg/4 arms of √2 Z₀ and a 2Z₀ resistor across the outputs: all ports matched, outputs isolated, −3.01 dB each and lossless when fed at the input.
A = 10 log(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) dB; matched pads in cascade add in dB; a pad must be rated for P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>out</sub>.
θ = (β₋ − β₊)L/2 in a biased ferrite; its sense is set by the bias, not by the direction of travel, so a round trip turns 2θ.
Isolator S = [0 0; 1 0]. Circulator S = [0 0 1; 1 0 0; 0 1 0]: matched and lossless but not reciprocal.
X = (βᵢV₁/2V₀)θ₀; the fundamental beam current peaks at X = 1.841, where J₁ = 0.582, so the two-cavity efficiency is at most 58.2 %.
V₀/(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)² = (2πN)²e/(8ω²L²m) with N = n − ¼ = ¾, 1¾, 2¾ …
B₀c = √(8V₀m/e)/[b(1 − a²/b²)]; above it, with no RF, electrons turn back before the anode.
A<sub>p</sub> = −9.54 + 47.3NC dB with C = (I₀Z₀/4V₀)<sup>1/3</sup>.
Transferred electrons give negative differential resistance above about 3.2 kV/cm in GaAs; transit-time mode f = v<sub>d</sub>/L with n₀L > 10¹² cm⁻².
Avalanche (90°) plus transit (90°) delay give negative resistance; f = v<sub>s</sub>/(2L<sub>d</sub>).
S = V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub> = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|); adjacent minima are λg/2 apart.
Short (Γ = −1), Open (+1), Load (0) and Thru standards remove the systematic errors of a vector network analyser at the reference plane.
Every transistor, resistor, capacitor, inductor and line formed in or on one semiconductor wafer, with no bond wires inside the chip.
C = ε₀εᵣA/d for the metal–insulator–metal sandwich; a spiral has series resistance R = ωL/Q with Q only about 10 to 20.

takeaways: At microwave frequencies waves, not voltages and currents, describe a network: b = S a, with S = Sᵀ for a reciprocal network and S†S = I for a lossless one.

A lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched at all ports, so a tee reflects, a resistive divider loses 6.02 dB per output, and a Wilkinson adds a resistor that works only for signals entering an output.
The magic tee and the rat-race are both 180° hybrids: sum at one port, difference at another, with those two ports isolated; the tee gets this from symmetry, the ring from path lengths.
A directional coupler is fixed by three numbers, and I = C + D: a 10 dB, 20 dB-directivity coupler sends 10 mW, 0.1 mW and 89.9 mW of every 100 mW to its coupled, isolated and through ports.
Decibels of power add along a chain: dBm − dB = dBm, and matched pads in cascade add their dB.
A biased ferrite breaks reciprocity; that is what makes an isolator absorb reverse power and a circulator stay matched and lossless as a three-port.

Tubes win on power: a klystron bunches a beam by velocity modulation (at most 58.2 % with two cavities), a magnetron works above the Hull cutoff field, and a TWT amplifies over an octave along a helix.

Solid-state sources work by negative resistance: Gunn f = v<sub>d</sub>/L at a few per cent efficiency, IMPATT f = v<sub>s</sub>/(2L<sub>d</sub>) with more power and more noise, tunnel diodes at microwatt levels.

Bench measurements are indirect: λg = 2 × (distance between adjacent minima), VSWR from V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub> (square-rooted for a power-reading detector), and S-parameters only after a VNA calibration.
An MMIC forms every part in one wafer: small, repeatable and broadband, but low in power and passive Q, and impossible to tune after fabrication.
bank_note: Long answers usually want the port numbering stated first, the S-matrix with its reciprocity and loss checks, and a closing number such as a power balance; calculation questions on tubes and diodes repeat the formulas in the key terms table.

bank.q: Define the scattering parameters of a two-port and the scattering matrix of an N-port. Explain why S-parameters are used at microwave frequencies, and state and prove the properties of the S-matrix of a reciprocal and of a lossless network.
outline: incident and reflected waves aᵢ, bᵢ; b = S a; Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ/aⱼ with other ports matched
meaning of S₁₁, S₂₁, S₁₂, S₂₂ and their dB forms
why: open and short terminations fail at microwave frequencies; matched loads are easy; |S|² is power
reciprocal: S = Sᵀ; lossless: S†S = I (unitary), with the power-balance proof
reference-plane shift: e<sup>−j(θᵢ + θⱼ)</sup>
a numerical check on a given matrix
answer: Waves at a port. At port i of a network with reference impedance Z₀, the incident wave is aᵢ = (Vᵢ + Z₀Iᵢ)/(2√Z₀) and the outgoing (scattered) wave is bᵢ = (Vᵢ − Z₀Iᵢ)/(2√Z₀). With RMS values |aᵢ|² is the power arriving at the port and |bᵢ|² the power leaving it.

Scattering matrix. For a linear N-port the outgoing waves depend linearly on the incoming ones: b = S a, where S is an N × N matrix. Its element Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ/aⱼ is measured with a wave fed into port j and every other port ended in a matched load, so that aₖ = 0 for k ≠ j.

answer.text: For a two-port:
answer.pre:
b₁ = S₁₁a₁ + S₁₂a₂
b₂ = S₂₁a₁ + S₂₂a₂

head: Parameter
Condition
Meaning
Usual dB form
rows: gain 20 log|S₂₁| or insertion loss −20 log|S₂₁|

answer: Why S-parameters at microwave frequencies. Z, Y and h parameters need open-circuit or short-circuit terminations. Above about 1 GHz an open end radiates and has fringing capacitance, a short has inductance, and both are hard to place at a defined plane; an active device may oscillate when its port is opened or shorted. Voltage and current are also not directly measurable on a waveguide. A matched load is easy to make, and directional couplers separate incident and reflected waves, so S-parameters are what a network analyser measures. They relate directly to power: |Sᵢⱼ|² is a power ratio.

answer.text: Reciprocal network (no ferrite, plasma or active device): S = Sᵀ. Proof outline: reciprocity gives Z = Zᵀ. With normalised impedances, S = (Z − I)(Z + I)⁻¹. Transposing, Sᵀ = (Z + I)⁻¹ᵀ(Z − I)ᵀ = (Z + I)⁻¹(Z − I) because Z is symmetric, and (Z + I)⁻¹ and (Z − I) commute (both are functions of Z). So Sᵀ = S, that is Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ.

Lossless network: S†S = I. Proof: the power entering is Σ|aᵢ|² = a†a and the power leaving is Σ|bᵢ|² = b†b = a†S†Sa. With no loss the two are equal for every a, so a†(S†S − I)a = 0 for all a, which forces S†S = I.
answer.pre:
Column form: Σᵢ |Sᵢⱼ|² = 1 for every j  (all power fed at j comes out)
             Σᵢ SᵢⱼS*ᵢₖ = 0 for j ≠ k  (columns orthogonal)

answer: Matched port i: Sᵢᵢ = 0. Reference planes: if port n is moved outward by βl = θₙ, every Sᵢⱼ is multiplied by e<sup>−j(θᵢ + θⱼ)</sup>, so Sₙₙ turns by 2θₙ and an off-diagonal term touching port n by θₙ.

answer.text: Numerical check, S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, S₁₂ = S₂₁ = 0.8∠−60°, S₂₂ = 0.3∠0°:

answer: Closing check: the matched lossless reciprocal two-port S = [0 1∠−90° ; 1∠−90° 0] (a quarter-wave line) passes all three tests: symmetric, columns 0 + 1 = 1, and columns orthogonal (0 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 0).

bank.q: Describe the E-plane tee, the H-plane tee and the magic tee. Derive the S-matrix of an ideal magic tee from its properties, and show how it works as a sum and difference hybrid.
outline: port numbering; branch on the broad wall (E-plane, series) or narrow wall (H-plane, shunt)
phase of the outputs when fed from the branch: 180° (E) and in phase (H)
magic tee: H-arm and E-arm on one junction; matched with a post and iris
derive S from symmetry, isolation, matching, reciprocity and losslessness
sum at the H-arm, difference at the E-arm; worked numbers
uses: balanced mixer, monopulse comparator, E-H tuner
answer: Tees. A waveguide tee is a three-port: ports 1 and 2 are the ends of the main (collinear) guide and port 3 is the branch. In the TE₁₀ mode the E-field runs across the narrow dimension of the guide.

E-plane tee (series tee): the branch is joined to the broad wall, so its axis lies in the plane of E. A wave fed into port 3 divides equally into ports 1 and 2, 180° apart, because the E-lines turn opposite ways into the two arms. Waves fed into 1 and 2 in antiphase add at port 3.
H-plane tee (shunt tee): the branch is joined to the narrow wall, in the plane of H. A wave fed into port 3 divides equally into ports 1 and 2 in phase. Waves fed into 1 and 2 in phase add at port 3.

answer.text: With the branch matched, the matrices are (rows and columns 1, 2, 3):

answer: Each column sums to ¼ + ¼ + ½ = 1, so the tees are lossless, but S₁₁ = S₂₂ = ½: a collinear port reflects a quarter of its power. That is forced, since a lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched at every port.
Magic tee. Put an E-arm (port 4) and an H-arm (port 3) on the same junction of the collinear guide (ports 1, 2), and add a matching post and iris so that ports 3 and 4 are matched.

answer.text: Derivation of S:
answer.pre:
1. Symmetry of the H-arm about the centre plane:  S₁₃ = S₂₃
2. Antisymmetry of the E-arm:                      S₁₄ = −S₂₄
3. E and H fields of different symmetry:            S₃₄ = S₄₃ = 0
4. Ports 3 and 4 matched:                          S₃₃ = S₄₄ = 0
5. Reciprocity:                                    Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ
6. Lossless, column 3:  |S₁₃|² + |S₂₃|² = 1  →  S₁₃ = S₂₃ = 1/√2
   Lossless, column 4:  |S₁₄|² + |S₂₄|² = 1  →  S₁₄ = −S₂₄ = 1/√2
7. Lossless, column 1:  |S₁₁|² + |S₂₁|² + ½ + ½ = 1  →  S₁₁ = S₂₁ = 0
   column 2 likewise:  S₂₂ = 0

answer.text: So all four ports are matched once 3 and 4 are, and ports 1 and 2 are isolated:

answer: Check: symmetric; every column holds two entries of 1/√2, so it sums to 1; columns 1 and 2 give (1·1 + 1·(−1))/2 = 0, columns 3 and 4 likewise. S is unitary.

answer.text: Sum and difference. From rows 3 and 4, b₃ = (a₁ + a₂)/√2 and b₄ = (a₁ − a₂)/√2. Example: 8 W and 2 W fed in phase into ports 1 and 2.

head: Quantity
Working
Value
rows: rows 1, 2 have no a₁, a₂ terms

answer: Uses: a balanced mixer feeds the signal into the H-arm and the local oscillator into the E-arm, so the two never couple to each other; a monopulse radar comparator forms sum and difference beams; an E-H tuner (sliding shorts on the E- and H-arms) matches an unknown load.
Closing check on power: 9 W + 1 W = 10 W = 8 W + 2 W, as a lossless matched device requires.

bank.q: Define coupling, directivity and isolation of a directional coupler and write the S-matrix of an ideal coupler. Explain the two-hole coupler, and how a hybrid ring gives an equal split with in-phase or 180° outputs.
outline: port names: input, through, coupled, isolated
C = 10 log(P₁/P₃), D = 10 log(P₃/P₄), I = 10 log(P₁/P₄) = C + D
ideal coupler S-matrix with α² + β² = 1 and its checks
two-hole coupler: λg/4 spacing, forward add, reverse cancel
rat-race: 1.5λg ring, arcs λg/4, 3λg/4, λg/4, λg/4; sum and difference ports by path difference
answer: Ports: 1 input, 2 through, 3 coupled, 4 isolated; all others matched when one is fed.

answer.text: Definitions (all positive dB):
answer.pre:
Coupling     C = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₃) = −20 log₁₀|S₃₁|
Directivity  D = 10 log₁₀(P₃/P₄) = 20 log₁₀(|S₃₁|/|S₄₁|)
Isolation    I = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₄) = −20 log₁₀|S₄₁| = C + D

answer: Coupling sets how big the sample is; directivity measures how well the coupler separates the forward wave from the reverse wave; isolation is the total attenuation from input to isolated port.

answer.text: Ideal coupler (matched, reciprocal, lossless, S₄₁ = 0), with |S₂₁| = α and |S₃₁| = β:
answer.pre: S = [ 0  α  jβ  0 ;  α  0  0  jβ ;  jβ  0  0  α ;  0  jβ  α  0 ],   α² + β² = 1

answer: Checks: S = Sᵀ; each column has α² + β² = 1; columns 1 and 2 give 0. For a 10 dB coupler β = 0.316 and α = √(1 − 0.1) = 0.949, a through loss of 0.46 dB.

Two-hole coupler: two holes λg/4 apart in a common broad wall. Towards port 3 both leaked waves travel the same total length and add. Towards port 4 their paths differ by 2 × λg/4 = λg/2, so they cancel, which gives the directivity. The cancellation is exact only at the design frequency; more holes with graded sizes widen the band.

answer.text: Hybrid ring (rat-race): a ring of circumference 1.5λg of √2 Z₀ line, ports numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 round it with arcs 1–2 = λg/4, 2–3 = 3λg/4, 3–4 = λg/4, 4–1 = λg/4. A wave fed in goes both ways; it adds where the two paths differ by a whole wavelength and cancels where they differ by λg/2.

answer: So port 1 is the sum port (outputs at 2 and 4 equal and in phase) and port 3 is the difference port (outputs equal and 180° apart); ports 1 and 3 are isolated from each other. Signals fed into 2 and 4 give their sum at 1 and difference at 3.
Closing check: 10 mW into port 1 of the ring gives 5 mW + 5 mW + 0 = 10 mW; in the 10 dB coupler, 100 mW in gives 10 mW coupled, 0.1 mW leaked (with D = 20 dB) and 89.9 mW through, 100 mW in all.

bank.q: Explain Faraday rotation in a biased ferrite. Describe the Faraday-rotation isolator and the three-port circulator, write their S-matrices, and show that the circulator is lossless but not reciprocal.
outline: ferrite properties; precession; tensor permeability; f₀ ≈ 28 GHz/T
linear wave = two circular waves; θ = (β₋ − β₊)L/2; sense set by the bias, round trip 2θ
isolator: 45° rotator, 45° twisted guides, resistive cards; forward and reverse paths
isolator S = [0 0; 1 0]; circulator S = [0 0 1; 1 0 0; 0 1 0]
circulator tests: unitary, matched, not symmetric; isolator from a circulator; numbers
answer: Ferrite: a ceramic of iron oxide with other metal oxides (for example YIG), an insulator with εr about 10 to 15 and low loss, but strongly magnetic.

Under a DC bias B₀ the electron spins precess about B₀ at f₀ ≈ 28 GHz per tesla. A microwave H-field rotating in the same sense as the precession couples strongly to the spins; one rotating the other way hardly does. The permeability is therefore a tensor: a right-circular wave sees μ₊ and a left-circular wave μ₋.

answer.text: Faraday rotation: a linearly polarised wave is the sum of two equal circular waves of opposite sense. They travel with phase constants β₊ and β₋, so after a length L the plane of polarisation has turned by

answer: The sense of the rotation is fixed by B₀, not by the direction of travel. A wave going forward turns by θ; reflected back, it turns a further θ in the same sense, so the round trip gives 2θ, not zero. That is nonreciprocity; a dielectric would undo its effect on the way back.

answer.text: Faraday-rotation isolator: rectangular guide → transition → circular guide with a ferrite rod giving 45° → transition → rectangular guide twisted 45°. A resistive card lies parallel to the broad wall at each end.

head: Direction
What happens
Result
rows: rotated +45°, lines up with the twisted output guide; E is normal to the card
rotated a further +45°, arrives at 90° to the input guide; E lies along the card

answer.text: Ideal isolator:

answer: It is not symmetric (nonreciprocal), and column 2 sums to 0, so it is lossy: the reverse power is turned into heat on purpose.

answer.text: Three-port circulator: a Y-junction of three guides or striplines at 120° over a biased ferrite post. Power entering 1 leaves at 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1; reversing the magnet reverses the rotation.
answer.pre: S = [ 0  0  1 ;  1  0  0 ;  0  1  0 ]   (row = output port, column = input port)

answer.text: Tests on the circulator matrix:

head: Test
Working
Result
rows: each column has one entry of magnitude 1; columns share no non-zero row, so are orthogonal

answer: So the circulator is a matched lossless three-port, which a reciprocal three-port can never be; giving up reciprocity is what makes it possible.

Isolator from a circulator: end port 3 in a matched load. Forward 1 → 2 passes; power returning into 2 goes to 3 and is absorbed. With 0.5 dB insertion loss and 25 dB isolation, 10 dBm in at port 1 gives 9.5 dBm at port 2, and 10 dBm fed into port 2 gives only −15 dBm at port 1.
Closing check: 9.5 dBm = 8.91 mW and −15 dBm = 0.032 mW, a ratio of 282, which is 24.5 dB = 25 − 0.5 dB, as the two specifications require.

answer: Two-cavity klystron. The gun accelerates electrons through V₀, so they reach the input cavity (buncher) at v₀ = √(2eV₀/m) = 0.593 × 10⁶√V₀ m/s. The RF input sets up V₁ sin ωt across the gap. Electrons crossing while the field retards them leave slower; those crossing while it accelerates leave faster: v = v₀[1 + (βᵢV₁/2V₀) sin ωt], with βᵢ the gap coupling coefficient.

In the drift space the faster, later electrons catch the slower, earlier ones, and the beam forms one bunch per cycle around the electron that crossed at zero field. Bunching is measured by X = (βᵢV₁/2V₀)θ₀, θ₀ = ωL/v₀; the fundamental beam current 2I₀J₁(X) is largest at X = 1.841.

The catcher cavity is placed where the bunches are densest and phased so that its field retards them: they give kinetic energy to the cavity, which delivers the amplified RF. The collector takes the spent beam. Efficiency η = β₀V₂J₁(X)/V₀ is at most J₁(1.841) = 58.2 %. Use: high-power amplifier in radar transmitters and particle accelerators (multicavity versions).

Reflex klystron. One cavity; behind it a repeller at −V<sub>R</sub> with respect to the cathode. The retarding field (V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)/L turns the electrons back through the same gap. Velocity modulation on the way out becomes bunching on the way back: faster electrons go deeper and return later, so the bunch forms around the electron that left when the gap field was going from accelerating to retarding.

answer.text: Derivation. Deceleration a = e(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)/(mL). An electron entering at v₀ returns after
answer.pre:
T′ = 2v₀/a = 2mv₀L / [e(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)]
For energy transfer the bunch must return when the gap field retards it most:
   ωT′ = 2πn − π/2 = 2π(n − ¼),  n = 1, 2, 3 …   i.e. N = ¾, 1¾, 2¾ …
Substituting v₀ = √(2eV₀/m):
   V₀ / (V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)² = (2πN)² e / (8ω²L²m)

answer.text: Example: V₀ = 600 V, L = 2 mm, f = 8 GHz gives V<sub>R</sub> + V₀ = 2643.3/N volts:

answer: Tuning: within a mode, a small change of V<sub>R</sub> shifts the return phase and pulls the frequency a little (electronic tuning); a screw that changes the cavity moves the centre frequency (mechanical tuning). The best efficiency of mode N is 2X′J₁(X′)/(2πN) = 22.7 % for N = 1¾. Use: local oscillator in radar receivers and laboratory signal source.

Closing check: for N = 1¾ the round trip is T′ = 1.75/(8 × 10⁹) = 0.219 ns; from the formula T′ = 2mv₀L/[e(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)] = 2 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.453 × 10⁷ × 0.002/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1510.5) = 0.219 ns. The two agree.

bank.q: A directional coupler has a coupling of 10 dB and a directivity of 20 dB, and 100 mW is fed into port 1 with every other port matched. Find the isolation, the power at the coupled, isolated and through ports, the through loss and |S₂₁|.
outline: isolation I = C + D
P₃ from C, P₄ from D (or I)
P₂ by power balance for a lossless coupler
through loss in dB and |S₂₁| = √(P₂/P₁)
closing power check
answer: Ports: 1 input, 2 through, 3 coupled, 4 isolated. The coupler is taken as lossless and matched, so the power fed in leaves by ports 2, 3 and 4 only.

answer.text: Isolation from the two given figures:
answer.pre:
I = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₄) = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₃) + 10 log₁₀(P₃/P₄) = C + D
I = 10 dB + 20 dB = 30 dB

answer.text: Coupled and isolated powers:
answer.pre:

Electronic tuning: within the 1¾ mode, a small change in V<sub>R</sub> moves the return phase away from the ideal value; the cavity then settles a little off its resonance, so the output frequency shifts by a few megahertz while the power falls off either side of the centre.

bank.q: Describe the measurement of VSWR with a slotted line. On a WR-90 guide (a = 22.86 mm) the VSWR of a load is 3 and adjacent minima are 22 mm apart. Find |Γ|, the return loss, the mismatch loss, the fraction of power reflected, the guide wavelength and the frequency.

VSWR = V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub>; square root for a power-reading detector; double-minimum method for high VSWR
|Γ| = (S − 1)/(S + 1); RL and mismatch loss
λg = 2d; 1/λ₀² = 1/λg² + 1/(2a)²

answer: Bench: a source (Gunn or klystron), an isolator so that reflections do not pull it, a variable attenuator to set the level, a cavity wavemeter, the slotted line, and the load under test. A thin probe enters a slot along the centre of the broad wall, where it cuts no wall current; it samples the E-field and feeds a crystal detector and a VSWR meter.

Procedure: slide the probe along the line and note the largest and smallest readings and the positions of two adjacent minima. If the meter reads voltage, VSWR = V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub>; if the detector is square law and the meter reads power, take VSWR = √(P<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>min</sub>). For a high VSWR (above about 10) the minimum is too shallow to read against the maximum, so use the double-minimum method: find the two positions either side of a minimum where the reading is twice the minimum, distance W apart, and S ≈ λg/(πW).

answer.text: Reflection coefficient and losses for S = 3:
answer.pre:
|Γ| = (S − 1)/(S + 1) = (3 − 1)/(3 + 1) = 0.5
Return loss = −20 log₁₀ 0.5 = 6.02 dB
Reflected fraction = |Γ|² = 0.25 = 25 %
Mismatch loss = −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²) = −10 log₁₀ 0.75 = 1.25 dB

answer: So a quarter of the incident power comes back, and the load receives three quarters of it, a 1.25 dB loss even though the load itself may be lossless in its own right.

answer.text: Guide wavelength: adjacent minima are half a guide wavelength apart.
Frequency. For TE₁₀ the cutoff wavelength is λc = 2a = 45.72 mm:
Results:

answer: The load impedance can also be found: measure the distance from the load to the first minimum and use the Smith chart or z<sub>L</sub> = (1 − jS tan βd)/(S − j tan βd).

Closing check: going back from |Γ| = 0.5, (1 + 0.5)/(1 − 0.5) = 3 = S; and 9.46 GHz lies inside the WR-90 band of about 8.2 to 12.4 GHz, above the 6.56 GHz cutoff (c/2a), so a guide wavelength of 44 mm is possible in this guide.

answer: Swept source: a synthesised oscillator stepped over the band. Switch: sends the test signal to port 1 (forward) or port 2 (reverse) and terminates the idle port in a matched load.

Couplers (test set): at each port a directional coupler pair samples the incident wave a and the outgoing wave b separately. Receivers: down-convert each sample to a low intermediate frequency and measure its amplitude and phase against the reference. Processor: forms the ratios and applies the error correction, then shows the results in dB, phase, Smith chart or time domain.

answer.text: What is measured:

answer: These are the four entries of the scattering matrix, b = S a, measured in magnitude and phase across the band.

Why calibrate: the raw ratios include the hardware. Finite coupler directivity leaks part of the incident wave into the reflected channel; the test ports are not perfectly matched (source match and load match); the cables and receivers do not track equally over frequency; and some signal leaks between ports. A full two-port has 12 such error terms per frequency, and they can be as large as the S₁₁ of a good device.

answer.text: SOLT calibration measures known standards at the reference plane (the end of the test cables) and solves for the error terms:

answer: A one-port model has three error terms (directivity, source match, reflection tracking), so three standards give three equations. After calibration the processor applies the correction to every sweep, and a check with a known airline or attenuator confirms it.

answer.text: Closing check: why the load term matters. Raw directivity 30 dB gives an error wave of 10<sup>−30/20</sup> = 0.0316. A device with |S₁₁| = 0.1 (return loss 20 dB) could then read anywhere between

answer: A spread of almost 6 dB on a 20 dB part shows that uncalibrated data cannot be accepted for a final S₁₁.

bank.q: Compare microwave tubes and solid-state sources. Which would you choose for a pulsed search radar needing 1 MW peak and for a 10 GHz motion sensor needing 10 mW? Support the choice with the DC power each needs.
outline: what limits each: electron beam in vacuum against a small semiconductor die
table: power, frequency, efficiency, voltage, size, life, noise, cost
radar: magnetron (or klystron for coherent radar); duty cycle and average power
sensor: Gunn diode; DC power and heat
closing numeric comparison
answer: Why the two families differ. A tube moves an electron beam through vacuum, where it can carry a large current at tens of kilovolts with nothing to overheat but the collector and anode, which can be large and cooled. A solid-state source makes its power inside a semiconductor a few micrometres thick: the transit length must be short for high frequency, the voltage is limited by breakdown, and the heat comes out through a tiny area. So tubes win on power at a given frequency, and semiconductors on size, voltage and life.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Tubes (klystron, magnetron, TWT)
Solid state (Gunn, IMPATT, tunnel)
rows: µW to about 1 W per device
magnetron 40 % to 70 %; two-cavity klystron at most 58 % in theory
Gunn a few %; IMPATT up to about 15 %; TRAPATT tens of %
a few volts to about 100 V
klystron low; magnetron noisy and incoherent
Gunn low; IMPATT high; tunnel very low
TWT an octave; cavity tubes narrow

answer: Pulsed search radar, 1 MW peak. No single diode comes close: the ratio is 1 MW against about 1 W, a factor of 10⁶. Only a tube gives this from one device. A magnetron is cheap, compact for its power and efficient, and suits a non-coherent search radar. If the radar must be coherent (pulse-Doppler, moving-target indication), a klystron amplifier or a TWT driven by a stable source is used instead, because each magnetron pulse starts with a random phase.

answer.text: DC power for the radar. Take a 1 µs pulse at 1 kHz repetition and a magnetron efficiency of 60 %:
answer.pre:
Duty cycle = 1 µs × 1000 /s = 0.001
Average RF power = 10⁶ W × 0.001 = 1 kW
Peak DC input = 10⁶ / 0.6 = 1.67 MW,  average DC = 1.67 kW
Heat in the tube = 1.67 − 1.00 = 0.67 kW (average)

answer: Motion sensor, 10 mW at 10 GHz. A Gunn diode in a cavity is the usual choice: it runs from a few volts, starts instantly, costs little, and its low noise helps the Doppler receiver. A tube here would be absurd: a heater alone would use more power than the whole sensor.

answer.text: DC power for the sensor at a Gunn efficiency of 2.5 %:
answer.pre:
P<sub>DC</sub> = 10 mW / 0.025 = 0.4 W  (for example 8 V at 50 mA)
Heat in the diode = 0.4 − 0.01 = 0.39 W, which a small heat sink removes

answer.text: Summary of the two choices:

head: Job
Source
RF out
DC in
Main reason
rows: only a tube reaches the power
low voltage, small, cheap, low noise

answer: Trend: solid-state transmitters now replace tubes in many radars by combining hundreds of GaN or GaAs amplifier modules, as in an active phased array, which also gives graceful failure (one dead module costs little). The single-device power gap remains, so very high peak power, high frequency, or cost per watt still favour tubes.

Closing check: the peak powers differ by 10⁶ W / 10⁻² W = 10⁸, which is 80 dB, while the average DC inputs differ by 1670 W / 0.4 W ≈ 4200, about 36 dB; the low duty cycle of the radar and the higher efficiency of the magnetron (60 % against 2.5 %) account for the gap closing by 44 dB.

answer: So the ring is a small printed pattern that fits in a microstrip circuit, while the magic tee belongs in a waveguide system and handles far more power.

Bandwidth. The magic tee isolates its E- and H-arms by symmetry, which holds at every frequency, so its isolation stays high across the guide band; its match depends on the post and iris and so is narrower. The rat-race works by path differences that are exact only where the arcs are exact fractions of λg. Away from the design frequency the cancellation at the isolated port is incomplete and the split drifts from equal, so the rat-race is the narrower-band device.

In a monopulse radar the two inputs come from two halves of the antenna: the difference falls to zero when the target is on the boresight, and its size and sign tell how far off and which way.

bank.q: Prove that a lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched at all its ports. Evaluate the ways a practical divider gets round this, and show with numbers how a Wilkinson divider for 50 Ω at 3 GHz (εeff = 2.8) behaves when fed at port 1, fed at an output, and when one output is mismatched with |Γ| = 0.2.
outline: assume matched, reciprocal, lossless; write S; unitary conditions; contradiction
ways out: allow loss (resistive, Wilkinson), allow nonreciprocity (circulator), accept mismatch (tee)
Wilkinson design: √2 Z₀ λg/4 arms, 2Z₀ resistor; S-matrix
three feeding cases with powers
judgement and closing power check

answer.text: Assume a three-port that is matched (Sᵢᵢ = 0), reciprocal (Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ) and lossless (S†S = I):
answer.pre: S = [ 0  S₁₂  S₁₃ ;  S₁₂  0  S₂₃ ;  S₁₃  S₂₃  0 ]

answer.text: Unitary conditions:
answer.pre:
Columns of unit length:  |S₁₂|² + |S₁₃|² = 1   (1)
                         |S₁₂|² + |S₂₃|² = 1   (2)
                         |S₁₃|² + |S₂₃|² = 1   (3)
Columns orthogonal:      S*₁₃S₂₃ = 0          (4)
                         S*₂₃S₁₂ = 0          (5)
                         S*₁₂S₁₃ = 0          (6)

answer: By (4) to (6) at least two of S₁₂, S₁₃, S₂₃ must be zero. Say S₁₃ = S₂₃ = 0: then (3) gives 0 = 1, a contradiction. Any other pair gives the same. So no such network exists: one of the three properties must go.

answer.text: Wilkinson design, Z₀ = 50 Ω at 3 GHz with εeff = 2.8 on the branch lines:
answer.pre:
Branch impedance = √2 × 50 = 70.7 Ω
λ₀ = c/f = 2.998 × 10⁸ / 3 × 10⁹ = 99.93 mm
λg = 99.93/√2.8 = 59.72 mm;  branch length λg/4 = 14.93 mm
Resistor = 2Z₀ = 100 Ω between the two outputs

answer.text: Its S-matrix (ports 1 input, 2 and 3 outputs):

answer: Column 1 sums to ½ + ½ = 1: fed at port 1 the divider is lossless. Columns 2 and 3 sum to ½ only: fed at an output, half the power reaches the input and half is absorbed. S₂₃ = 0: the outputs are isolated. S is symmetric: the divider is reciprocal. So it keeps matching and reciprocity and gives up losslessness only for a wave entering an output, which the proof allows.

answer.text: Three cases with 10 mW:
Working for the mismatched case: port 2 receives 5 mW and reflects |Γ|² = 0.04 of it.
answer.pre:
Reflected = 0.04 × 5 = 0.2 mW, entering port 2
Of that: |S₁₂|² = ½ → 0.1 mW back to port 1;  |S₃₂|² = 0 → nothing to port 3
          the remaining 0.1 mW is absorbed in the 100 Ω resistor

answer: Judgement: for an equal split with matched, isolated outputs the Wilkinson is the best of the reciprocal options: no loss in normal use, and a fault at one output does not disturb the other. Its limits are bandwidth, since the branches are a quarter-wave only near 3 GHz (more sections widen it), and the resistor, which must be rated for the power a mismatched output sends back. Where power is high or the band very wide, a resistive divider (lossy) or a magic tee or rat-race with a load on the fourth port is used instead.

Closing check for the mismatched case: 5 (port 3) + 4.8 (load on port 2) + 0.1 (back to port 1) + 0.1 (resistor) = 10.0 mW, the input; and port 3 still gets exactly 5 mW, showing the isolation S₃₂ = 0 at work.

glossary.def: A terminal pair or waveguide opening where power enters or leaves a microwave network.
A load whose impedance equals the reference impedance, so no wave reflects from it.
The position on each port line at which the incident and outgoing waves are defined; moving it by βl changes the phase of S.
A network whose scattering matrix is symmetric, Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ; any network without ferrite, plasma or active devices.
A network that absorbs no power; its scattering matrix is unitary, S†S = I.
−20 log₁₀|Γ| dB: how far the reflected wave is below the incident one.
−20 log₁₀|S₂₁| dB: the loss in transmission through a two-port.
A four-port waveguide hybrid with an E-arm and an H-arm on one junction; all four ports matched, E- and H-arms isolated, collinear arms isolated.
D = 10 log₁₀(P₃/P₄) dB, how well a coupler separates the forward wave from the reverse wave.
A 1.5λg ring hybrid (rat-race) whose sum and difference ports are opposite each other and isolated.
A three-port divider with quarter-wave arms and an isolation resistor, matched at all ports with isolated outputs.
A T or π resistor network that gives a set loss in dB while presenting Z₀ at both ports.
A magnetic ceramic insulator whose permeability becomes a nonreciprocal tensor under a DC magnetic bias.
Turning of the polarisation plane of a wave in a biased ferrite, in a sense set by the bias.
A ferrite multi-port that routes power in a fixed cyclic order, such as 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1.
Speeding up and slowing down electrons of a beam by an RF gap voltage, so that they later form bunches.
The negative electrode of a reflex klystron that turns the beam back through its cavity.
The magnetic field (or voltage) at which magnetron electrons just graze the anode with no RF present.
A helix or coupled cavities that slow the RF wave to about the beam speed in a TWT.
A part of a device curve where current falls as voltage rises, so the device can feed power to a resonator.
A Gunn mode in which the field swings through the negative-resistance region faster than a domain can form; the cavity sets the frequency.
A diode detector whose output is proportional to RF power, that is to the square of the RF voltage.
A calibrated instrument that measures the magnitude and phase of S-parameters over frequency.
A plated metal strap that crosses over other lines on an MMIC with air underneath, so with little capacitance.
A monolithic microwave integrated circuit: all active and passive parts made in or on one semiconductor chip.
